vpp0.title: VoltPulse
vpp0.w1: VoltPulse is a compact IoT device designed for the remote monitoring of mains power availability and the transmission of data to a remote server, providing access to information via Telegram. VoltPulse is optimized for autonomous, energy-efficient operation in environments with unstable power supply.
vpp0.w2: The repository contains two directories. The first holds the firmware for the device's operation and data transmission to a personal computer. The second contains a Python script that allows reading and saving this data.

vpp1.title: What is VoltPulse?
vpp1.t1: The energy and security situation in Kyiv has remained challenging for quite some time. October this year has brought plenty of familiar "surprises": residential buildings can be left without electricity for hours, sometimes even half a day.
vpp1.t101: Recently, a friend of mine shared a fairly simple idea: it would be great to have a device that could remotely check whether there is electricity at home. After all, many everyday decisions depend on it — from charging a phone to preparing dinner. The idea immediately caught my attention. I had already explored a similar concept while working on LockedNet — an autonomous "Anti-Blackout" ecosystem designed for use during power outages. However, back then, I focused primarily on the system architecture rather than the practical implementation of its hardware components. So this time, I decided to start practically from scratch.
vpp1.t102: I recently completed another project — BaryCore, an ecosystem of agents for remotely managing a workspace through Telegram. And it seemed like an excellent foundation for this new development. Why build a separate communication system and interface when an existing infrastructure can already receive user commands, process them, and return results? All I need is to extend it with a new agent responsible for monitoring the power supply.
vpp1.t103: The main question remained: where could I obtain reliable information about the state of my home's electrical supply? The obvious answer might seem to be power outage schedules. However, during emergency shutdowns and damage to energy infrastructure, the actual situation does not always match the published schedule. And I don't need a forecast or a probability. I need to know whether I'll be able to make some delicious mashed potatoes with cutlets and relax in a hot bath tonight, or whether I'll have to buy some sandwiches on my way home and dig out a washbasin from the balcony.
vpp1.t104: Therefore, the source of information must be a physical device directly connected to the home's electrical supply. It will detect the presence of power and transmit the corresponding status to the software system.
vpp1.t105: I currently plan to cover the development of VoltPulse in three articles. The first focuses on the concept and system architecture, the second on the hardware and device assembly, and the third on firmware development, integration with BaryCore, and practical testing. I don't plan to revisit the architecture of my previous projects in detail. If you're interested, you can explore them in the corresponding sections of NovTech.
vpp1.t2: Meet VoltPulse — Remote Power Monitoring System. It is a compact, autonomous device designed to monitor the availability of electricity in a home's power supply. Its main task is to periodically detect the power status and transmit the collected data to BaryCore, allowing users to retrieve the information through Telegram. A new static-type Analytic Agent — SVP (VoltPulse) — will be created within BaryCore. Unlike general-purpose agents, it will have only one specialized function: reporting the current state of the home's power supply using the command "@SVP voltage".
vpp1.t201: This way, VoltPulse will not depend on power outage schedules or third-party forecasting services. Its own physical sensor will serve as the source of information, while BaryCore will act as the communication interface.
vpp1.t3: I have already revised the hardware concept several times. The components, measurement logic, and even the basic principle of detecting the power supply status have changed along the way. Initially, I considered measuring the actual voltage rather than simply obtaining a logical result of "power available / power unavailable". Eventually, I decided to settle on a simpler architecture. For this particular task, accurately measuring the household mains voltage is unnecessary.
vpp1.t301: The configuration presented below is still conceptual. During assembly and testing, individual components or circuit design decisions may change.
vpp1.t302: The device will be built around an ESP32-C3 microcontroller with Wi-Fi support and Deep Sleep capability. Its logic circuitry will operate at a regulated voltage of 3.3V. To reduce power consumption, the controller will spend most of its time in sleep mode. Every 300 seconds, it will wake up, determine the external power status, measure the battery voltage, transmit telemetry, and return to sleep. This approach should significantly reduce average energy consumption. Of course, information about the power supply will not be updated instantly, but I consider this delay acceptable for everyday household use.
vpp1.t303: The power source will be an 18650 lithium-ion battery with a nominal capacity of 3000 mAh. For preliminary calculations, I assume a usable capacity of 2700 mAh, although the actual value depends on various factors. Since the battery voltage changes during discharge, a Pololu S7V8F3 voltage regulator will be installed between the battery and the microcontroller. It can maintain a 3.3V output as long as the input voltage remains within its operating range.
vpp1.t304: Another task will be monitoring the remaining battery charge. For this purpose, the microcontroller's built-in ADC will measure the battery voltage through an appropriate resistive voltage divider. The firmware will provide an approximate charge percentage based on the nonlinear relationship between battery voltage and state of charge. I will use 4.2V as the upper reference point and 3.3V as the lower one.
vpp1.t305: Power consumption will still be present in Deep Sleep mode due to the voltage regulator and voltage divider. According to the documentation and preliminary calculations, the estimated current consumption is 75μA.
vpp1.t306: Let's estimate how long VoltPulse could theoretically operate without recharging.
vpp1.q4306: Operating time t = 2700 mAh / 7.43mA ≈ 363 h ≈ 15 days. The actual operating time may be shorter due to lower real-world efficiency.
vpp1.t307: To monitor the external power supply, I plan to use a standard USB power adapter that converts 230V AC into an isolated 5V DC output. The ESP32-C3 itself will have no direct electrical connection to the 230V mains. Instead, the adapter's output status will be detected using an optocoupler.
vpp1.t308: An optocoupler consists of an LED and a phototransistor, with information transmitted between them optically. This provides galvanic isolation between the adapter's signal circuit and the microcontroller's logic circuitry.
vpp1.t309: On the input side of the optocoupler, the LED will be connected to the USB adapter output through a current-limiting resistor. With a supply voltage of 5V, an LED forward voltage drop of 1.2V, and a resistance of 1kΩ, the current will be I = 3.8/1000 = 3.8mA.
vpp1.t310: The output side of the optocoupler will be connected to the microcontroller's GPIO4. To establish the required logic levels, a pull-up to 3.3V is planned, activated during measurement through GPIO5.
vpp1.t311: The power detection logic will be inverted:
vpp1.q0311: × Power available = the adapter provides 5V = the optocoupler LED emits light, the phototransistor turns on and pulls GPIO4 to ground = a LOW signal is detected, corresponding to voltage = true.
vpp1.q1311: × Power unavailable = the phototransistor is off = thanks to the pull-up, GPIO4 reads a HIGH signal, corresponding to voltage = false.
vpp1.t4: The microcontroller will operate in a repeating cycle. After waking from Deep Sleep, the device will initialize the necessary peripherals, read the logic level on GPIO4, and measure the battery voltage through the ADC. The resulting signal will be converted into a Boolean value called voltage, while the measured battery voltage will be converted into an approximate charge percentage.
vpp1.t401: Next, the microcontroller will establish a Wi-Fi connection and transmit both parameters to the cloud server. Once transmission is complete, the device will return to Deep Sleep for a specified period.
vpp1.t402: A lightweight service will be deployed on a virtual machine to receive data from VoltPulse. Its task will be to accept messages from the microcontroller and update a JSON state file. In addition to voltage and battery, the server will record the timestamp of the last successfully received telemetry update. This will help determine whether the reported power status is still current.
vpp1.t403: Access to the telemetry receiver will be restricted through device authentication, while data transmission will use a secure communication channel. For now, I do not plan to implement a full database or measurement history. For this particular task, storing only the latest received state is sufficient: each new transmission will replace the previous values.
vpp1.t404: On the BaryCore side, the changes will be minimal. A new method will be added to the Analytic Agents' tools module to handle requests from the SVP agent. It will read the current JSON state and generate a response for the user. Therefore, the BaryCore ecosystem itself will not directly poll the physical device. Instead, it will work with data already received and prepared by the server.
vpp1.t5: At this stage, the overall system concept has been established, its main components have been identified, and the device's expected battery life has been preliminarily estimated. The practical implementation comes next.

vpp2.title: Prototyping and Testing
vpp2.w: In the previous article, I introduced the VoltPulse concept, explored its main hardware components, and explained how they interact. Now it's time to move from theoretical architecture to practical implementation: assembling a prototype, writing the firmware, configuring data transmission, and conducting the first system tests.
vpp2.t1: For the initial implementation of VoltPulse, I decided to use a modular architecture, the principles of which I had already discussed in the previous article. This approach makes it possible to verify the functionality of individual components and the entire system before moving on to designing the final device.
vpp2.t101: During development, I built two versions of the prototype. The first was assembled on a universal prototyping board, with components soldered manually, electrical connections formed using solder, and external contacts provided for connecting additional modules. However, this construction turned out to be quite fragile, especially considering the need to repeatedly reconnect components during development.
vpp2.t102: So I eventually moved on to a second version — a circuit based on the same operating principles, but assembled on a solderless breadboard. This made it much easier to introduce changes, check connections, and experiment with individual components.
vpp2.t103: Both prototypes implement exactly the same logic. At this stage, their main purpose is not compactness or aesthetics, but verifying that the chosen architecture works as intended.
vpp2.t2: The system can be divided into three levels: the physical VoltPulse device, a cloud-based Virtual Machine (VM), and the BaryCore ecosystem. Each performs a separate task, while communication between them is handled through network protocols.
vpp2.t201: The device's firmware essentially turns VoltPulse into a real sleepyhead. It spends most of its existence in Deep Sleep mode, minimizing battery consumption. Only periodically does the microcontroller wake up, perform the necessary measurements, transmit data, and return to sleep.
vpp2.t202: After each wake-up, the ESP32-C3 initializes the necessary peripheral modules. The first operation is measuring the battery voltage — before establishing a Wi-Fi connection, which helps eliminate the effect of voltage drops caused by significant current consumption on the measurement result. For this purpose, I use the analogReadMilliVolts() function provided by Espressif in the development environment. It returns the measured voltage at the ADC input in millivolts, taking the analog-to-digital converter's calibration into account. However, the ADC receives only half of the actual battery voltage after it passes through the resistive voltage divider. To restore the original battery voltage in volts, the result is additionally scaled by a factor of 2/1000.
vpp2.t203: The resulting value is passed to the BatteryChargeCalculation function, which estimates the remaining battery charge as a percentage. This introduces a separate challenge. The relationship between a lithium-ion battery's state of charge and its voltage is nonlinear, and its exact shape depends on the characteristics of the specific cell, temperature, load, and other factors. Building an accurate model would require lengthy experimental measurements over discharge cycles. However, such precision is not critical for my application. So I used publicly available reference data on typical lithium-ion battery characteristics. Based on this information, I created a set of reference points describing the relationship between voltage and charge level, stored them in an array, and implemented a linear interpolation algorithm between neighboring values. As a result, the function returns an approximate battery percentage. Of course, this estimate does not guarantee high accuracy. But for me, there is no fundamental difference between, say, 75% and 58% if I'm coming home in a few hours and the device could potentially keep running for several more days.
vpp2.t204: Next, the microcontroller sets GPIO5 to a HIGH logic level, activating the pull-up of the measurement input. Depending on the state of the optocoupler's phototransistor, GPIO4 receives one of two logic levels — HIGH or LOW. After reading the signal, GPIO5 stops supplying the control signal, and the resulting value is converted into a Boolean parameter called voltage. The detection logic is inverted: LOW indicates that external power is available, while HIGH indicates its absence. I explained the reasoning behind this decision in the previous article.
vpp2.t205: Once all the necessary measurements are complete, the device moves on to the next stage. The ESP32-C3 connects to the home Wi-Fi network. After establishing the connection, the microcontroller prepares a message containing two main parameters: voltage — the power supply status, and battery — the estimated remaining battery charge. These data must then be transmitted to the cloud-based virtual machine.
vpp2.t206: To provide access to the server-side components, I use the Caddy web server as a reverse proxy. It receives external HTTPS requests and forwards them to an internal service responsible for processing telemetry. It also enables secure TLS connections. Therefore, the ESP32-C3 sends data to a specified address, Caddy routes the request to the telemetry receiver, and the receiver processes the incoming message and updates the corresponding JSON state file.
vpp2.t207: The complete software implementation, including the firmware and server-side components, is available in the project's GitHub repository.
vpp2.t208: I didn't create a separate user interface for VoltPulse because, as I emphasized in the previous article, the necessary infrastructure already exists — BaryCore Sky. Since VoltPulse data are already stored on the same machine, all that remains is to organize their retrieval and delivery to the user. To accomplish this, I extended the Analyst Agents' tools module with a new function. It opens the JSON state file, retrieves the required parameters, and transforms them into a readable message, including the correct display of the last measurement timestamp.
vpp2.t209: Next, I created a new agent called SVP (VoltPulse) and gave it access to this function. To receive the status report, simply send the command "@SVP voltage".
vpp2.t3: After completing the assembly and programming, it was time to check whether the entire system worked as intended. I identified three main testing scenarios: verifying data transmission to the virtual machine, checking battery voltage measurements, and testing the detection of the home's power supply status.
vpp2.t301: For the first test, I created a separate copy of the firmware in which the battery and voltage values were hardcoded directly into the program. This allowed me to test the network functionality independently of the sensors and other hardware components. Only the ESP32-C3 development board was connected to the computer, without any additional components. After launching the firmware, the microcontroller established a connection to the server and transmitted the test values to the JSON state file.
vpp2.t302: For the second test, I returned the microcontroller to its rightful place — the fully assembled prototype. This time, the device was powered by its battery but was not connected to the USB power adapter. Therefore, the expected result had two parts: the system should report the absence of mains power while correctly transmitting the estimated battery charge. As a result, the SVP agent successfully displayed the received information in Telegram.
vpp2.t303: The final test involved connecting the prototype to a wall outlet through the USB power adapter. At the time of testing, electricity was available in the building. Therefore, the optocoupler was expected to switch to the corresponding state, while the microcontroller should detect a LOW logic signal and interpret it as voltage = true. The result:
vpp2.t4: The VoltPulse prototype has been successfully assembled and tested. However, using the device as a collection of modules, connecting wires, and a breadboard is not the most convenient solution for permanent operation. Therefore, the next stage will be designing a custom printed circuit board, ordering its manufacture, and manually soldering the components. This means the current circuit will require significant redesign. And it's not simply a matter of transferring the existing connections onto a PCB.
vpp2.t401: First, I plan to replace the ready-made development board with a standalone ESP32-C3-WROOM-02 module. Although this decision requires additional circuit design work, it will optimize the PCB layout and eliminate some of the auxiliary components installed on the development board.
vpp2.t402: Another issue to resolve is battery placement. One option is to keep the 18650 cell outside the main PCB and provide a suitable connector for attaching a battery holder. Alternatively, I could switch to a different lithium-ion battery format, allowing me to optimize the board's physical design.
vpp2.t403: The PCB will also need a USB connector for the external power adapter, which provides the signal indicating whether mains electricity is available.
vpp2.t404: Resolving these questions and designing the PCB itself will be the next stage of VoltPulse development.

vpp3.title: PCB Modeling
vpp3.w: In the previous chapters, I explored the VoltPulse architecture, assembled a prototype, implemented the software, and tested the system's operation. The device can now detect the presence of mains power, estimate the battery charge level, and transmit telemetry to a cloud server, where the collected data becomes accessible through the BaryCore ecosystem. The next stage of development was designing a custom printed circuit board — PCB. For this, I used KiCad, a software suite for designing electronic schematics and printed circuit boards. The process involved several stages, which I will cover in this chapter.
vpp3.t1: The first challenge was not simply transferring the existing connections from the breadboard onto a PCB, but rethinking the device's hardware design. The VoltPulse prototype consisted of ready-made modules, each of which already included some of the necessary electronics. Designing a custom PCB meant moving away from this modular approach and implementing the corresponding circuits directly on the board.
vpp3.t101: First, I replaced the development board with a standalone ESP32-C3-WROOM-02 module. It contains the microcontroller, the necessary radio-frequency components, and an antenna, but lacks the additional supporting circuitry normally provided on a ready-made development board.
vpp3.t102: The schematic now includes a dedicated USB-C connector for programming the microcontroller through its built-in USB interface. I also added RESET and BOOT buttons for controlling the startup process, along with additional supporting components to ensure stable operation of the logic circuitry. Particular attention was paid to the 3.3V power rail. Capacitors were placed near the microcontroller to filter the power supply and compensate for short-term fluctuations in current consumption.
vpp3.t103: Another change was the transition to surface-mount components (SMD). For resistors and ceramic capacitors, I chose the 0603 package size, which significantly reduced the board area required for passive components.
vpp3.t104: Next comes the second major circuit block. The prototype used a ready-made Pololu S7V8F3 voltage regulator. For the final PCB, I decided to replace it with an integrated TPS63031 buck-boost converter, which will provide a regulated 3.3V output. The key advantage of a buck-boost architecture is its ability to both step down and step up the input voltage. This is important when powering the device from an 18650 battery, whose voltage changes throughout the discharge cycle. Unlike the ready-made module, however, the TPS63031 requires its own external supporting components. Following the manufacturer's documentation, I added a 1.5 μH inductor, input and output capacitors, and the necessary connections between the IC pins. This circuit became one of the most demanding parts of the PCB layout.
vpp3.t105: I decided to keep the battery separate from the main PCB. To connect it, I included a two-pin screw terminal block that can be used with an external 18650 battery holder. In addition to the main power path, I implemented a battery voltage monitoring line through a resistive voltage divider, allowing the ESP32-C3 to continue estimating the remaining charge using its built-in ADC.
vpp3.t106: The final functional block is responsible for detecting the presence of mains power. Its operating principle remains the same as in the prototype. An external USB power adapter converts 230V AC into isolated 5V DC, while a PC817 optocoupler makes it possible to detect the presence of this voltage without a direct electrical connection between the adapter's output and the microcontroller's logic circuitry.
vpp3.t2: Most components were assigned standard footprints from the KiCad libraries. However, I had to create a custom footprint for the inductor based on its physical dimensions and solder pads.
vpp3.t201: I placed the ESP32 module in the upper part of the board, leaving the required clearance around its antenna. The RESET and BOOT buttons, along with the microcontroller's supporting components, were positioned nearby. Below them, I arranged the power supply section around the TPS63031 and its supporting circuitry, while the battery terminal block was placed near the board's edge. On the right side, I positioned two USB-C connectors: one for programming the ESP32-C3 and the other for connecting the external mains power adapter. The optocoupler was placed between these connectors and the other main circuit blocks.
vpp3.t202: In a schematic, two components can be connected by a single line regardless of their physical positions. On a PCB, things are more complicated: every connection has a physical geometry, and traces cannot simply cross one another on the same copper layer. For this version, I therefore chose a two-layer PCB. This allowed me to use both the top and bottom copper layers, with plated through-hole vias providing connections between them.
vpp3.t203: I paid particular attention to the TPS63031's supporting circuitry. The inductor and capacitors were placed close to the IC, while the power traces were made wider than ordinary signal traces. I also created a ground plane on the bottom layer of the PCB. This approach provides a common ground connection for the relevant circuit blocks without having to route a separate long trace to every ground pin.
vpp3.t3: The Gerber files for PCB manufacturing have been prepared, along with the Bill of Materials (BOM) and Component Placement List (CPL) required for organizing the subsequent assembly process. The next task is to finalize the manufacturing files and order the physical PCB. Once the board arrives and is assembled, I plan to share the result in a LinkedIn post.
